analysis.one_liner: Bans hidden 'spread pricing' markups by pharmacy benefit managers in Medicaid and requires drug payment details be made public.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee's Health Subcommittee for the rest of the 117th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: When a state Medicaid program buys prescription drugs through middlemen called pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs), those PBMs sometimes charge the state more than they actually pay the pharmacy, pocketing the difference — a practice called 'spread pricing.' This bill would require PBMs to pass drug payments through to pharmacies in full, limit what they can charge for administration, ban spread pricing, and publish detailed information about drug prices, discounts, and dispensing fees. It would also extend funding for the government's survey of what pharmacies actually pay for drugs.
analysis.who_benefits: State Medicaid programs and taxpayers, who would stop paying hidden middleman markups on prescription drugs; Medicaid patients, who benefit from pharmacies staying in the program; and community pharmacies, which would be paid what they are actually owed instead of having payment skimmed by PBMs.

how_it_helps.text: Requires Medicaid drug payments to be made on a pass-through model: every dollar for a drug must go in full to the pharmacy that dispensed it, and the PBM's cut is limited to a reasonable administrative fee [S3].

Explicitly bans spread pricing — any amount the PBM charges the state above what it pays the pharmacy, including post-sale fees and adjustments — from being counted for federal matching payments [S3].
Forces PBMs to open their books to states and the federal government, disclosing all ingredient costs, dispensing fees, discounts, rebates, and any other remuneration [S3].

Requires pharmacies receiving Medicaid-related payments to respond to the national drug acquisition cost survey and requires the resulting price data, response rates, and dispensing fee averages to be published [S3].
Bars states and Medicaid managed care plans from prohibiting 340B clinics and their contract pharmacies from dispensing discounted drugs to Medicaid patients [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pharmacy benefit managers and the insurers that hire them, which would lose the margin they earn on the difference between what states are charged and what pharmacies are paid.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pharmacy benefit managers and Medicaid insurers

drawbacks.text: The bill adds compliance work: every community pharmacy that receives any Medicaid-related payment would be required to respond to price surveys, and states would have to collect and publish detailed reporting [S3].

Banning spread pricing constrains how PBMs are paid but does not itself cap the underlying price of drugs; if PBMs raise their allowed administrative fees, total drug spending could shift rather than fall, which is why the bill tries to limit admin fees to 'reasonable cost' [S3].

A pass-through mandate changes the reimbursement mechanics for Medicaid managed care plans and PBMs mid-contract-cycle, and opponents of similar measures have argued it reduces plans' flexibility to negotiate drug costs; the bill's effective date is 18 months after enactment to soften that transition [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and concrete: Medicaid — a program jointly funded by federal and state taxpayers — would stop paying hidden markups to intermediaries on every prescription, and independent pharmacies that serve Medicaid patients would stop losing money on fills. The costs are mostly administrative (survey and reporting work for pharmacies and states) and the bill leaves drug list prices themselves untouched, so it addresses the middleman skim rather than the root cause of high drug prices. It is a narrow, targeted transparency fix, not a broad drug-price solution.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which sent it to its Health Subcommittee, and nothing further happened before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Buddy Carter, a Republican from Georgia who worked as a pharmacist, and Rep. Vicente Gonzalez, a Texas Democrat, introduced the bill on December 1, 2021 [S1].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and the next day to that committee's Subcommittee on Health [S5].
It drew only four cosponsors — one Democrat and three Republicans — and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote in the House [S4], [S5].
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so the bill died with no action beyond referral [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmacy benefit managers and Medicaid managed care insurers keep their current spread-pricing arrangements, while Medicaid programs and community pharmacies continue under the reimbursement rules the bill would have changed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pharmacy benefit managers kept the status quo

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a Republican with a Democratic cosponsor, and the small cosponsor list split 1 Democrat to 3 Republicans; no votes were ever taken, so no partisan roll-call record exists.

industries.note: The bill's central target: it would bar PBMs from keeping the spread between what Medicaid pays and what pharmacies receive, cap their admin fees, and force them to disclose every discount and fee. Spread pricing is a core PBM revenue source, and losing it would directly reduce their Medicaid business margins.

Plans that take responsibility for drug coverage would have to comply with the same pass-through rules for their PBM contracts, ending a flexible arrangement that let them profit on drug reimbursement spreads. Compliance costs rise, though the bill does not change what they can charge states for premiums.

Pharmacies would receive the full Medicaid payment for each prescription instead of having part skimmed off, and the bill extends the federal survey funding that sets their reimbursement benchmarks. Independent pharmacies, which spread pricing hits hardest, benefit most.

industries.industry: 340B covered entities (safety-net hospitals and clinics) and their contract pharmacies
industries.note: The bill prohibits states, insurers, and PBMs from barring 340B discounted-drug dispensing in Medicaid, protecting a revenue stream these safety-net providers rely on.
